{"type":"ReadFile","FileContent":{"content":"1→### OpenAPI 3.1 contract and contract tests for REST v1 (PLAN2.P6.3)

- Added: `openapi/vaulter-v1.yaml` — the OpenAPI 3.1 contract of the whole REST API v1 (81 operations; `operationId`
  is the route name without `vaulter.v1.`): parameters, `If-Match` (`428`/`412`) and `If-None-Match` (`304`) rules,
  cache and file-delivery headers, `application/problem+json` errors with their `code` values, a schema for every
  resource, and `openapi/examples/*.json` — one real response per resource (PLAN2.D64).
- Added: contract tests. Every `vaulter.v1.*` route has an operation and the other way round (same method and path);
  the `core`, `drive` and `documents` feature tests run with `VAULTER_OPENAPI_VALIDATE=1`, so every v1 response is
  validated for status, headers, media type and body with `opis/json-schema` (draft 2020-12; the adapter stops on a
10→  construct it cannot judge instead of skipping it); a golden `routes-v1.json` pins the route list.
- Added: `.github/workflows/openapi.yml` — `oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR` against the contract of the last
  released tag (the base branch before the first release that carries the file), with a pinned `oasdiff` version.
- Fixed: `GET nodes/{node}?include=children` answered an empty `properties` of a child as `[]`; it is `{}`, as in
  every other node (found by the response validation).
- Docs: `reference/rest-api` (en, ru) explains the contract, the checks and the compatibility policy of `v1`;
  CONTRIBUTING describes how to change the contract.

{"type":"ReadFile","FileContent":{"content":"1→Валидаторы, предусловия и кэширование (C07, D62)

ETag узла — валидатор ПРЕДСТАВЛЕНИЯ для вызывающего: `"{id}.{sequence}.{digest}"`, digest = первые 16 hex sha256 канонического JSON базового представления Node этого вызывающего без поля etag (ключи рекурсивно отсортированы, json_encode JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES|JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE|JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION). Учитывает всё, что фактически возвращается: abilities, scan_status, viewer.starred, presentation, properties, файл/документ голову. Клиент обязан считать ETag непрозрачным (не парсить sequence). Класс Vaulter\Http\Support\RepresentationTag: `node(array $representationWithoutEtag, string $id, int $sequence): string`, `document(string $nodeId, int $epoch, int $stateVersion): string`.

ETag содержимого документа (D35): `"{nodeId}.{collab_epoch}.{state_version}"` — допустим без дайджеста, т.к. представление content не содержит полей, зависящих от вызывающего; тест обязан доказать идентичность тела и ETag для двух ролей (reader и writer).

Где выдаётся: заголовок ETag — только GET nodes/{node} без include и GET documents/{node}/content, а также ответы мутаций, возвращающих Node/контент; поле etag — в каждом Node (включая элементы списков). Ответ с include не несёт заголовка ETag (другая вариация).

If-Match (Vaulter\Http\Support\Preconditions):
10→1. Маршруты IM (см. #Routes): нет заголовка → 428 precondition_required (meta.header = "If-Match"); `*` → 428 (meta.reason = "wildcard_not_allowed"); слабый W/ → 412 (сильное сравнение не проходит).
2. Порядок: аутентификация → резолв drive/узла (tenant) → Operations find + авторизация (нет View → 404, нет способности → 403) → вычисление текущего представления → сравнение If-Match (список через запятую — совпадение любого) → мутация с expectedSequence = текущий sequence (узел) или expectedStateVersion = текущий state_version (документ). Несовпадение → 412 node_sequence_mismatch / document_state_mismatch (meta.node_id). Гонка между проверкой и записью ловится атомарным CAS Operations (тот же 412, P4.7 writer map).
3. Нигде If-Match не обходит авторизацию; 412 не раскрывает текущий ETag и не выдаётся вызывающему без View (сначала 404).
Неизменённые PHP-сигнатуры: expectedSequence/expectedStateVersion в PHP API остаются необязательными (C07).

If-None-Match → 304: только GET nodes/{node} и GET documents/{node}/content; после полной авторизации и карантинной проверки; слабое сравнение; 304 несёт ETag, Cache-Control, Vary, X-Vaulter-Api-Version, X-Request-Id, без тела. Скачивания и списки 304 не выдают.

Cache-Control:
- JSON одиночного ресурса с ETag: `private, no-cache`; Vary: Authorization, Cookie.
- Списки, мутации, сессии коллаборации, ответы с token/secret, ошибки, 428: `no-store` (+private для GET).
20→- Скачивания/экспорт/302 direct: `private, no-store`.
- Публичные шары: `private, no-store` + Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.","content_concise":"1→Валидаторы, предусловия и кэширование (C07, D62)

{"type":"ReadFile","FileContent":{"content":"1→Problem Details (P6.2, D29, OPUS 10 §6)

Контракт: Vaulter\Exceptions\Contracts\ProblemException получает третий метод `problemDetails(): array` (meta-поля; по умолчанию []); код и статус — как сейчас. Трейт Vaulter\Exceptions\Concerns\ProvidesProblemDetails даёт реализацию по умолчанию; существующие renderExtras() переносятся в problemDetails() (ConcurrentUpdateException, OffsetMismatchException и др. — найти grep -rn "renderExtras\|function render(" packages/*/src).

Рендерер: Vaulter\Http\Problems\ProblemRenderer (core) регистрируется в VaulterServiceProvider через $this->app->make(ExceptionHandler::class)->renderable(fn (Throwable $e, Request $r) => $renderer->render($e, $r)). Срабатывает, только если $request->route()?->getName() начинается с 'vaulter.v1.' ИЛИ путь начинается с versionedPrefix().'/' (для 404/405 до матчинга маршрута). Хостовые маршруты не затрагиваются. VaulterException::render() удаляется в P6.8 (до этого обслуживает легаси-маршруты прежним телом {message, code}).

Тело (application/problem+json):
{"type": "https://github.com/axiomasoft/vaulter/blob/main/docs/reference/errors.md#<code>", "title": <lang>, "status": <int>, "code": <code>, "detail": <lang с плейсхолдерами из meta> | null, "request_id": <X-Request-Id>, "errors": <Laravel errors map> | null, "meta": <problemDetails()> | {}}.
Заголовки: Content-Type: application/problem+json, Content-Language: <app()->getLocale()>, Cache-Control: no-store, X-Vaulter-Api-Version: 1, X-Request-Id; 429 — Retry-After (из ThrottleRequestsException headers); 405 — Allow.
10→Сообщение исключения (Why/Fix/Docs) не уходит клиенту как detail (D29); detail берётся только из lang. meta проходит allowlist: запрещены ключи path, storage_key, tenant_id, token, sql, trace, file, line, password, secret (рекурсивно) — нарушение удаляет ключ и пишет warning в лог (тест ProblemMetaRedactionTest).

Маппинг фреймворк-исключений (только для v1):
| Исключение | status | code |
|---|---|---|
| AuthenticationException, MissingActorException | 401 | actor_required |
| AuthorizationException (Gate) | 403 | permission_denied |
| ValidationException | 422 | validation_failed (errors = $e->errors()) |
| ThrottleRequestsException | 429 | rate_limited |
| NotFoundHttpException без маршрута / ModelNotFoundException | 404 | route_not_found / node_not_found |
20→| MethodNotAllowedHttpException | 405 | method_not_allowed |
| PostTooLargeException | 413 | payload_too_large |
| HttpException прочие | его статус | http_<status> |
| любое иное Throwable | 500 | internal_error (detail null; исключение report()) |

Новые коды фазы (стабильный контракт): precondition_required 428 (PreconditionRequiredException, core), route_not_found 404, method_not_allowed 405, payload_too_large 413, internal_error 500, http_<status>, drive_not_found 404 (существующий StorageNotFoundException проверить код; если иной — привести к drive_not_found с записью в UPGRADE), api_version_mismatch (только клиентский, @vaulter/vue). Полная таблица кодов = OPUS 10 §6 ∪ P4-design#Errors ∪ P5-design#Errors ∪ эта; генерируется в docs/reference/errors.md из реестра.

Реестр кодов: Vaulter\Http\Problems\ProblemCatalog::all(): array<string, array{status:int, exception:class-string|null, package:string}> — единственный источник для docs/reference/errors.md (генерация командой vaulter:errors:reference {--check} {--path=*} по образцу core/src/Console/EventsReferenceCommand.php + core/src/Events/EventsReference.php (P5.2): маркеры <!-- vaulter:errors:start --> / <!-- vaulter:errors:end -->, страницы docs/reference/errors.md и docs/ru/reference/errors.md) и для OpenAPI (P6.3 перечисляет коды в Problem.code examples). Пакеты drive/documents регистрируют свои коды через тег контейнера vaulter.problem_codes (провайдер пакета), core не импортирует их классы.

Тест ProblemCatalogLangTest: каждый код имеет title en и ru.

{"type":"ReadFile","FileContent":{"content":"1→Карта маршрутов v1 (OPUS 10 §4 + D65)

Имя = vaulter.v1.<имя>; путь относительно /{prefix}/v1. «IM» — обязателен If-Match (428/412, #Validators). Контроллеры core — Vaulter\Http\Controllers\…, drive — Vaulter\Drive\Http\Controllers\…, documents — Vaulter\Documents\Http\Controllers\….

CORE (P6.1), стек authenticated:
| Метод путь | Имя | Контроллер | Operations | Ответ |

# Working with long-running background tasks

Only submitting or queuing jobs is not sufficient to complete the task. The definition of done is the job has completed successfully and you have verified that it has produced all the expected outputs.
10→
This means you must see through the jobs completion by watching the job to ensure that its healthy, progressing, and working as intended.

## Tools available

There's two ways to watch jobs: monitor and loop. Decide which of the two you need, sometimes you need both.

### monitor — deterministic, actionable events

- Use a monitor when the event is a predicate a script can evaluate — an API response, an exit code, a port answering.
20→- Typical events: CI turning red, a PR comment or merge conflict, a PR becoming ready to merge, a dev server coming up or going down, a job reaching a terminal state.
- The monitor requires a script polls on a fixed cadence and stays silent until the predicate fires, so an idle job costs nothing. More on writing good monitoring scripts below.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Monitoring a PR — wake on CI breaking, merge conflicts, etc.
  - Checking if local tooling is up — wake on the service being unavailable, errors, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases can be checked deterministically.

### loop — qualitative health that needs reading

- Use a loop when judging health requires reading the logs and system information to detect failing, faulty or stalled jobs. It uses a subagent which is more expensive but more thorough.
30→- Typical signals: the loss curve going unstable, a filtering pipeline producing garbage, throughput quietly degrading, faulty nodes throwing CUDA errors.
- A subagent reads the logs on a fixed cadence (say every 10 min) and reports what changed, so it costs a wakeup every cycle.
- Examples of when to use:
  - Checking on a training or data processing job — the subagent should scan for instability, degradation, faulty nodes, etc.
  - Monitoring system deployment health — the subagent should scan for 4xx/5xx, response times, resources, etc.
  - All of these wakeup cases are hard to describe deterministically and hard to fully enumerate, so it is better to use a subagent to validate.

## Good monitoring scripts

The monitor tool wakes you up every time you log to stdout. Wakeups are expensive, so only log if there is something actionable — but log it as early as possible, since staying silent delays the task. Plan accordingly: minimize the number of wakeups while still firing them as quickly as possible.
40→
### Planning

- Enumerate all terminal conditions.
  - For PRs, this includes the PR being merged or closed.
  - For long-running jobs, this includes the job completing or unrecoverable failures.
- Enumerate all other situations where a wakeup is needed.
  - For PRs, this would include when a comment arrives (there are four different types of PR comments), when CI fails, when a merge conflict arises, and when the PR becomes ready to merge (CI green, no conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers).
  - For an ML training job, this can be when the loss is unstable or the instance is preempted.
- Determine situations where the monitoring has to update what it is tracking. For example, for monitoring PRs, the latest commit hash may change as you push new commits.
50→
### Writing

- The monitoring script should poll every 30s. `watch_pr.py` defaults to
  `--poll-interval 30`. Lower intervals cause GitHub rate limits, especially
  with more than one watcher on the same token.
- Based on the planning, exit immediately on terminal conditions with FAILED, DONE, or CANCELLED, and log ACTION_REQUIRED for wakeups.
- Send all debug diagnostics — both your watcher's own trace and the monitored job's output — to a file, so a log line can never be mistaken for DONE, FAILED, or CANCELLED.
- The script should fail as early as possible. Emit a FAILED token immediately when any required condition reaches terminal failure. For example, if you are waiting on CI and any of them fail, emit FAILED immediately.
- Write the script to a durable location such as ~/.grok and name it something clear such as `ci_watcher.sh`.
60→- Key every log file the script writes on the pid or session id of the thing being watched. The paths are otherwise fixed, so a second job of the same kind silently clobbers the first one's log.

## Handling wake-ups

- Address errors or actionable events immediately. Look through the logs and debug the issue thoroughly before settling on a root cause, as long-running processes are generally expensive. Resubmit the job once it is fixed:
  - For PRs, this means repushing the changes and restarting CI (if needed).
  - For jobs, requeue or relaunch the job.
  - Always restart the monitor or loop so that it points at the new PR or job.
- If there are multiple jobs running, start debugging immediately when any jobs fail. Minimize total wall-time with completing tasks.

70→## Restarts

- Whenever you relaunch a job, always update the monitor.
- Monitors have a maximum 10-hour time limit, so be sure to restart them if you hit the time limit and if the task being monitored is still running.
- When you spawn a new monitor, make sure to kill any previous ones that the new one replaces. For example, if you fix a training run and respawn it, be sure to kill previous monitors, as irrelevant wakeups are expensive.

- If a monitor is in a terminal state, kill the monitor, the loop, and the job. Dangling processes such as unkilled broken training runs are expensive. Then, address all issues if present.

### Example: maintaining a dev server

run_terminal_command(
90→  command="echo $$; npm start >~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_$$.log 2>&1",

done

  - All of these wakeup cases are hard to describe deterministically and hard to fully enumerate, so it is better to use a subagent to validate.

## Good monitoring scripts

The monitor tool wakes you up every time you log to stdout. Wakeups are expensive, so only log if there is something actionable — but log it as early as possible, since staying silent delays the task. Plan accordingly: minimize the number of wakeups while still firing them as quickly as possible.

### Planning

- Enumerate all terminal conditions.
  - For PRs, this includes the PR being merged or closed.
  - For long-running jobs, this includes the job completing or unrecoverable failures.
- Enumerate all other situations where a wakeup is needed.
  - For PRs, this would include when a comment arrives (there are four different types of PR comments), when CI fails, when a merge conflict arises, and when the PR becomes ready to merge (CI green, no conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers).
  - For an ML training job, this can be when the loss is unstable or the instance is preempted.
- Determine situations where the monitoring has to update what it is tracking. For example, for monitoring PRs, the latest commit hash may change as you push new commits.

### Writing

- The monitoring script should poll every 30s. `watch_pr.py` defaults to
  `--poll-interval 30`. Lower intervals cause GitHub rate limits, especially
  with more than one watcher on the same token.
- Based on the planning, exit immediately on terminal conditions with FAILED, DONE, or CANCELLED, and log ACTION_REQUIRED for wakeups.
- Send all debug diagnostics — both your watcher's own trace and the monitored job's output — to a file, so a log line can never be mistaken for DONE, FAILED, or CANCELLED.
- The script should fail as early as possible. Emit a FAILED token immediately when any required condition reaches terminal failure. For example, if you are waiting on CI and any of them fail, emit FAILED immediately.
- Write the script to a durable location such as ~/.grok and name it something clear such as `ci_watcher.sh`.
- Key every log file the script writes on the pid or session id of the thing being watched. The paths are otherwise fixed, so a second job of the same kind silently clobbers the first one's log.

## Handling wake-ups

- Address errors or actionable events immediately. Look through the logs and debug the issue thoroughly before settling on a root cause, as long-running processes are generally expensive. Resubmit the job once it is fixed:
  - For PRs, this means repushing the changes and restarting CI (if needed).
  - For jobs, requeue or relaunch the job.
  - Always restart the monitor or loop so that it points at the new PR or job.
- If there are multiple jobs running, start debugging immediately when any jobs fail. Minimize total wall-time with completing tasks.

## Restarts

- Whenever you relaunch a job, always update the monitor.
- Monitors have a maximum 10-hour time limit, so be sure to restart them if you hit the time limit and if the task being monitored is still running.
- When you spawn a new monitor, make sure to kill any previous ones that the new one replaces. For example, if you fix a training run and respawn it, be sure to kill previous monitors, as irrelevant wakeups are expensive.

## Cleanup

- If a monitor is in a terminal state, kill the monitor, the loop, and the job. Dangling processes such as unkilled broken training runs are expensive. Then, address all issues if present.
- If an outdated monitor wakes you — that is, it is attached to an old or dead run — make sure to kill it.
- Do not leave detached workers, duplicate pollers, or orphaned watcher processes behind.

## Examples

### Example: maintaining a dev server

Suppose you just made some changes to the user's frontend code and would like to spin it up to test it. While you're testing it, you would like to know if the server goes down for any reason (if you made changes, for example). This is a great use case for the monitor tool. First start a React app in a background terminal, which reports its pid:

```
run_terminal_command(
  command="echo $$; npm start >~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_$$.log 2>&1",
  timeout=0,
  description="Start the dev server on :3000",
  background=true
) # prints the pid 123456789
```

There are no terminal states, but there are two actionable events from the watcher: `http://localhost:3000` coming up and going down.

You want to be notified as soon as it is up so you can use it, and you want to be woken when it stops so you can address it — fix the code, restart the server, free the port. Both down paths quote the tail of the server's log, so the wakeup arrives with the error already in hand. Polling every 5s is a good cadence since you want to quickly fix it if it is down, and it is not expensive to poll.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Log paths are keyed on the server pid so two dev servers cannot clobber each other.
PID=$1 URL=http://localhost:3000 DIR=~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks
LOG=$DIR/dev_server_$PID.log
up() { curl -fsS -o /dev/null --max-time 5 "$URL" 2>>"$DIR/watch_dev_server_$PID.log"; }
why() { tail -20 "$LOG" | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' '; }

until up; do
  kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null || { echo "FAILED: pid $PID exited before $URL came up: $(why)"; exit 1; }
  sleep 5
done
echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is up"

while :; do
  sleep 5
  up || { echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $URL is down: $(why)"; until up; do sleep 5; done; }
done
```

To spawn the monitor, point it at the pid `npm start` reported:

```
monitor(
  command='bash ~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/watch_dev_server.sh 123456789',
  description="Watch the dev server on :3000"
)
```

On the first wakeup the app is ready to use and you can start testing it. After that, you may be woken up if the server goes down. When you do:
- Read `~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/dev_server_<pid>.log` for the full compile error or port conflict and fix it.
- If the dev server survived, hot reload picks the fix up and the watcher recovers on its own, so leave the monitor running.
- If the process is dead, restart it with a fresh `run_terminal_command`, then kill this monitor and spawn a new one against the new pid.

### Example: PR monitoring

PR monitoring should stop when the PR is merged or closed, and it should wake up on:
- For comments, you should ask users how they would like to resolve them (which ones to address automatically, whether to respond / resolve, etc.), then store the decision for new future sessions. There are four different types of PR comments.
  - Inline review threads
  - Review bodies
  - Conversation comments
  - Commit comments
- Failing CI - most can be fixed in the code but sometimes they may be flaky. For flaky CI, just rerun them.
- Merge conflicts
- The PR becoming ready to merge — CI passes, no merge conflicts, reviews complete, no blockers, no unresolved inline threads. That wakeup is `kind: mergeable`. Tell the user they can merge now. It is not terminal; keep watching until merge or close.

You can find the example script bundled with this skill at watch_pr.py. It needs an authenticated `gh` CLI (`gh auth login`) and `python3`. Default poll is 30s; a lower poll rate may hit GitHub rate limits at higher concurrency. Transport errors (timeouts, resets, DNS) retry with backoff and jitter and do not print a line.

```
monitor(
  command='python3 ~/.grok/long-running-background-tasks/watch_pr.py "https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build/pull/123"',
  description="Watch PR 123"
)
```

### Example: training monitoring

For monitoring long training jobs, the terminal conditions are when the job either fails or completes. Further, many issues cannot be caught deterministically, so use a subagent to run a script for most of the high-level update, then scan the logs for errors such as faulty nodes or CUDA warnings.

The script below is bundled with this skill as watch_training.py. Run it with `--help` for every flag and for the run-directory and log-line layout it expects, since it parses nanoGPT stdout out of a Slurm run dir.

```md
Keep an eye on the nanoGPT run nanogpt_owt_124m_r1 (slurm job 1234567) and tell me what changed since last time. Worktree ~/worktrees/nanogpt-owt-124m.

1. python3 ~/.grok/skills/long-running-background-tasks/watch_training.py --run-name nanogpt_owt_124m_r1 --job-id 1234567 --target-val 3.00

How to report:
- Start with the job's state and if it changed, e.g. "still RUNNING" or "PENDING -> RUNNING".
- Copy the ISSUES line and the STATUS line from the monitor exactly as it is written, numbers and all. STATUS will include where the run is heading: how far along, iters left, the eta, and whether val loss is still coming down. We want val loss at or under 3.00.
- If the state didn't change, tell me that in one line and stop.
- If the job has finished or died, give me the state, the exit code, and the last ISSUES, and run these two for me:
  sacct -j 1234567 -D -X -P -o JobID,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Elapsed,NodeList,FailedNode
  tail -20 ~/train_logs/slurm-nanogpt_owt_124m_r1-1234567.out

Keep <=10 lines: state, progress and eta, loss trend, then anything that smells like training going unstable (loss spiking, NaN, val loss creeping back up) or the cluster misbehaving (a drained or failing node, OOM, NCCL errors, a preemption, iters suddenly slower than usual).
```

Launch the scheduler on a 10 min interval, and spawn a monitor to be notified when the job crashes or succeeds.

```
scheduler_create(
  interval="10m",
  prompt: "...", # Copy from the prompt above.
)
monitor(
  # Wakes on pending/running/finished changes after the first observation.
  # First poll is silent unless the job is already COMPLETED or failed —
  # PENDING matches *ING, so treating an empty previous state as a
  # transition would wake immediately on a just-submitted job.
  command='J=1234567; p=; while :; do s=$(sacct -nXP -j $J -o State|head -1); s=${s%% *}; s=${s:-PENDING}; if [ "$s" != "$p" ]; then case $s in COMPLETED) echo "DONE: $J"; exit;; PENDING|RUNNING|CONFIGURING|COMPLETING|REQUEUED|SUSPENDED|RESIZING) [ -n "$p" ] && echo "ACTION_REQUIRED: $J $p -> $s";; *) echo "FAILED: $J $s"; exit 1;; esac; fi; p=$s; sleep 30; done',
  description="Watch training run"
)
```

Launch both, so that we know when the job completes. When the monitor reports that the job has completed, cancel both the monitor and the scheduler, then determine next steps. Then:
- If it succeeded, simply present the results to the user.
- If it failed, debug the issue thoroughly, then fix and relaunch the job with new monitors attached. Make sure to have a thorough understanding of the issue before resubmitting, since training jobs are expensive. But always relaunch jobs so you don't waste the user's time.

  - APP_KEY="base64:lRknxO3IznrZODHVPvLNKylvYP19ch+EXZ8dM+i3OlY="

  - VAULTER_COLLAB_DRIVER="hocuspocus"

SharedNodeResource exposes `$node->created_at` directly. That value may be a Carbon object rather than an ISO string.

Laravel's Carbon typically serializes to ISO 8601 via JsonSerializable. The spec does not require a date-time format for PublicNode created_at, so the value may include microseconds without violating the contract. However, if json_encode uses a default encoder instead of Laravel's, Carbon could serialize as an object rather than a string.

Laravel's JsonResponse uses Carbon's jsonSerialize, which returns a string in recent versions. Public share tests pass validation, confirming the format matches the schema.

Public show returns `children` as null, while listing returns it as an array. The schema may not distinguish these two operations.

The design mandates date-time for all timestamps, but the public node schema omits that format. This creates a possible gap if Carbon defaults to non-RFC3339 strings.

Next I will inspect headers, problem schemas, Node required fields and additionalProperties, and the download, 304, and upload sections.

I will write a probe script to expose blind spots. The passing tests confirm that `created_at` is a string, not a Carbon object. I also noticed that `archived_at` is missing from the Drive resource, though the design requires it; this may be an out-of-scope drift if the resource was already accepted in P6.7.

I will audit design versus spec mismatches against actual routes and resources, not the spec itself. I will only report clear violations of item rules or contradictions with P6-design that lack a recorded deviation.

I am now inspecting headers and problem schemas, and I plan to dump all operations with a script.

One validator bug is confirmed: Node allows extra properties, so adding file_id passes validation.

I identified four more validator blind spots to prove. A date-time format may be ignored when combined with an array type. Header schemas can be skipped when the value is a numeric string and the schema uses a $ref. Body validation is intentionally bypassed for HEAD requests even when the content-type is application/json and inspectBody is false. Streamed JSON responses skip body validation entirely, which I will verify with a unit-level test.

Running a standalone Pest test outside the repository is impractical because Pest requires the test file to live inside the suite. Bootstrapping Laravel manually is too heavy. The simplest proof for validator bugs will be a PHP script that directly instantiates the validator classes.

A probe script in /tmp that bootstraps Orchestra Testbench is too heavy. The middleware exemption blind spot therefore remains unproven.

I am exploring lighter ways to prove the middleware blind spot. I could run Pest with a filter on `OpenApiValidationEnabledTest` or use `scripts/php84 vendor/bin/testbench` with a custom command. A separate `/tmp` script that only exercises the validator would isolate the bug without bootstrapping the full application.

I also noticed the probe prefix `vaulter.v1.__probe` is dangerously broad. It matches real route names like `vaulter.v1.__probes`, so any operation name starting with `__probe` would be silently exempted from validation. I will check the golden file to see if any actual routes use this prefix.

The `__probe` prefix is intentionally broad. It matches the probe route itself and any nested operation under it, such as `vaulter.v1.__probe.nodes.show`. This is by design. I will check the actual probe route names to confirm the pattern.

I verified that `$this->getJson()` triggers `terminate`, so validation runs in feature tests. PHPUnit correctly surfaces exceptions thrown during `terminate`, including those after `assertOk()`. I also noted that the middleware is registered via `pushMiddleware` inside `defineEnvironment`.

`pushMiddleware` appends to the global stack, so `terminate` still runs in reverse order. The enabled test confirms the middleware is registered. Laravel's `env()` helper should be available during `defineEnvironment`.

I am now inspecting the Opis validator's URI resolution and fragment encoding. I also noticed that when a response is a `$ref`, the schema pointer is rewritten to the referenced component path, which may affect how validation errors are reported.

The validator escapes slashes and tildes in schema pointers, but leaves plus signs untouched. The `application/problem+json` media type therefore becomes the fragment segment `application~1problem+json`. Percent-decoding of `%2B` back to `+` preserves the plus sign, so the fragment resolves correctly.

I verified that `*/*` media types survive fragment encoding and decoding correctly. I also considered whether Opis might fail to decode `%7E` before JSON pointer parsing, but the passing self-tests suggest it handles these pointers properly.

I am now hunting for false positives that pass validation incorrectly. I will inspect the Opis validator source for format and unevaluated-properties handling. I also noticed the Content-Disposition header schema may only require a string type without a pattern, so an invalid disposition value would slip through.

The Content-Disposition header schema only requires a string type, not a strict pattern. This is a minor gap if the header must be present but not validated against a specific format.

A more serious validator bug was found: Problem response schemas use `examples` instead of an `enum` for the `code` field. The validator therefore accepts any string code, while tests only check that the examples list matches the catalog.

The `code` field uses `examples` rather than `enum`, so the validator correctly accepts any string. This is per the design, not a bug. A response containing a typo code would therefore pass validation without being caught.

The document test sorts the catalog and asserts an exact match with the schema examples. Symfony YAML parsing order is therefore irrelevant.

Hub routes use camelCase identifiers such as userId and schemaVersion, which aligns with the resource specification. The OpenAPI test catalog includes codes from bootstrapped packages, so dynamically added codes would not appear in the spec. I also noted that comment anchor types are object or null.

The document content type schema allows an empty array, which is a minor looseness. Node additionalProperties and required fields against resource keys will be checked next. The size_bytes integer type is compatible with PHP int.

I am now hunting for concrete bugs. I also want to verify whether `sha256` is required in the file schema, since the design marks it optional.

I confirmed that `JsonResponse` correctly encodes the nested page response shape, with `children` becoming a `stdClass` object containing `data` and `meta`. Empty arrays remain arrays, null values stay null, and `getData()` returns only the body.

The `children` wrapper schema correctly matches the page response shape. Extra keys such as `links` would pass validation if `additionalProperties` is not explicitly disabled, but this is not a failure.

content.thinking:
A potential bug was noticed in Cache-Control constant values.

The design specifies `private, no-cache` for JSON single resources with ETag, but the spec constant is `no-cache, private`. This reversed order would cause validation failures if the code sends the design value. I need to check what the code actually emits.

The spec constant `CacheControlStore` is also reversed: it is `no-store, private` instead of the design's `no-store` plus private for GET and `private, no-store` for downloads. The design lists four distinct Cache-Control patterns for different response types.

The `CacheControlError` constant is an enum of `no-store` or `no-store, private`. The code might already match the spec order, so I still need to verify actual emitted header values.

A separate ETag mismatch was spotted: the schema enforces quoted strings via `^"[^"]+"$`, but the body `etag` field uses plain string without that pattern. Symfony's `setEtag()` adds quotes to the header, which could create a discrepancy between the body and header values.

A Vary header contradiction was found. The design requires `Vary: Authorization, Cookie` for single resources, but the spec omits this header entirely. If the code sends it, the contract simply does not validate it.

The missing Vary header is a spec incompleteness, not a validator hole. Severity is minor if the code sends it.

Content-Language on errors and the Allow header for 405 responses are also absent from the spec. The contract should document these design requirements.

Retry-After is an integer schema type but not required.

A potential bug has been identified.

The `errors` field correctly maps to a JSON object when validation errors are present, and to null when empty. The `meta` field is properly typed as an object with an empty `stdClass` fallback.

The `meta` schema permits arbitrary properties. The `errors` object type accepts array values without issue. A potential type mismatch was noted for `meta.next_cursor`: the schema expects a non-nullable string, but the cursor value may not always be a string.

The `created_at` field in `SharedNodeResource` is a Carbon instance. Laravel converts it to a string for JSON responses, but the schema only permits `string|null` without a date format.

The children collection returns an `AnonymousResourceCollection`, which may not match the expected array type.

Webhook delivery status is typed as a plain string without an enum. The code returns a database value that is likely a string column, so this should be acceptable.

The `last_status_code` field correctly maps to `integer|null`.

The upload protocol enum includes `direct`, but the code may never return that value. If it does, tests will fail.

A potential schema mismatch was spotted in `Node.properties`: property values inside the namespace object are typed as objects.

The `Node.properties` schema is sound. Each namespace object allows arbitrary JSON values, and the code stores strings as required.

`viewer.props` correctly serializes to an object or empty object.

The `capabilities` field requires boolean values. I need to verify that `NodeCapabilities::toArray` returns exactly the keys specified in the schema.

I am checking whether the public share show response uses `PublicNodeEnvelope` or a different structure with session token headers. I also need to verify if `Referrer-Policy` and `X-Share-Session` are required.

The `Problem.errors` object type correctly rejects JSON arrays, which is acceptable since the API returns objects or null.

I will inspect `SnapshotValue::iso` to check how fractional seconds are formatted.

SnapshotValue::iso produces valid JSON Schema date-time strings with or without fractional seconds.

A potential header validation bug was noted: nullable date-time fields might fail null checks if validators incorrectly enforce the format annotation. Tests should catch this if share expires_at is null.

A concrete bug was found in `documentedMediaType`: the YAML content map key `*/*` is likely misinterpreted by Symfony as an alias or invalid key.

The `*/*` content map key is properly quoted as `'*/*'` in the YAML, so Symfony does not misinterpret it as an alias. Exact MIME type matches correctly override `*/*`, and non-JSON bodies are skipped while headers are still validated. Inline MIME types such as `image/svg+xml` do not trigger false substring matches against `json`.

Downloads are streamed with `inspectBody` disabled, so a JSON file served as `application/json` passes the contract test without body inspection. The media type check falls back to `*/*`, and the response headers must still satisfy requirements such as disposition. A validator hole exists when the content-type header is missing, but downloads always include it.

302 redirects correctly match the `text/html` media type and skip body validation. The `Location` header is required and present, and the `X-Vaulter-Api-Version` header is set by middleware if it runs. I am now checking whether `Referrer-Policy` is included on file 302 responses.

Cache-Control on 302 redirects is correctly normalized to `no-store, private` by the middleware, matching the specification.

The `uploads.tus.head` contract documents status 204, which conflicts with the design.

The controller's `head` method must be inspected to determine whether the spec or the code is wrong. The design also specifies 204 for OPTIONS.

The tus protocol specification requires HEAD to return 200 OK with no body, not 204. This confirms the spec's 204 status is a deviation from the standard.

HEAD returns 204. The spec requires 204.

The design route table specifies 200 for HEAD, but the code and OpenAPI spec both correctly document 204. This is a pre-existing deviation, not a P6.3 bug. The review will focus on validator blind spots and genuine spec-code mismatches.

Upload-Length is correctly optional on HEAD. The Tus-Resumable header must be verified as 1.0.0. The Location header is always set on create, which is acceptable since it is not required. X-RateLimit headers are optional and may be absent or coerced.

The rate limit header schema expects integers, but Laravel's throttle middleware may emit strings such as empty values. This would cause validation failures when the headers are present.

The HEAD response returns 204 without an ETag. Laravel's `isMethodSafe()` returns true for HEAD, and `isSuccessful()` accepts 204, so the response bypasses the ETag cache-control logic.

HEAD responses correctly receive `Cache-Control: no-store, private` because HEAD is treated as a safe method. PATCH 204 responses correctly receive `no-store` since PATCH is not safe.

The review will now probe problem error types for empty validation arrays, and inspect Opis format, additionalProperties, allOf, and specific schema bugs.

PublicNodeResource returns Eloquent Carbon objects for created_at and updated_at. Laravel's JsonResponse relies on Carbon's JsonSerializable implementation, which is configured via a global serializeUsing callback. The review is checking whether this produces ISO-8601 strings or raw Carbon instances in the API response.

If Laravel's global `Carbon::serializeUsing` callback is unset, Carbon's `JsonSerializable` returns a raw array with date and timezone fields instead of an ISO-8601 string. The review is checking whether the resource layer casts or converts these Carbon instances to proper strings before they reach the API response.

Carbon 3's `jsonSerialize` returns an ISO-8601 string when a global serializer is configured, or a raw array otherwise. The public share tests will reveal whether the API response contains a string or an object for `created_at`. If the tests pass, the value is valid and no issue needs to be raised.

PublicNodeResource omits `format: date-time` on `created_at` and `updated_at`, unlike other resources. This is a minor inconsistency because the design requires all timestamps to be date-time, but it only matters if probes reveal an actual schema drift.

The Comment anchor field is typed as `object|null`. If the value is a JSON array of positions, validation fails.

The Hub load response schema restricts `content` to `object|null`, but some document types may return an array. The documents store request schema also requires `content` as `object`, while the underlying `DocumentBody` type allows arrays; the adapter does not validate this mismatch.

The review will probe whether document types return arrays for content, since the schema currently requires objects. It will also test validator edge cases where `errors` is an empty object instead of null, and inspect how operation statuses map to thrown exceptions. A probe will verify `OpenApiContract::at()` behavior with property names containing `~` or `/`, and check for fragment encoding bugs when schema keys are altered by `rawurlencode` but not decoded before pointer lookup.

A synthetic schema probe will test keys containing `~` and `{` to verify pointer resolution. The `JSON_BIGINT_AS_STRING` flag is not a practical bug because normal integers remain integers and oversized values become strings that fail integer validation. PHP's `json_decode` returns floats for JSON numbers like `1.0`, which may cause schema integer checks to reject them depending on the implementation.

NodeWithIncludes allOf is valid. The base Node schema allows additional properties, so a node without breadcrumb or children still satisfies the envelope. When children is present, it must match the NodePage schema.

The `getData()` fix correctly converts empty arrays to `{}` so children page nodes pass object validation. A potential issue remains: `JsonResponse` may preserve nested `stdClass` properties as `{}` when encoding the parent array.

The review will inspect `NodeResponses::page` to confirm that paginated nodes are wrapped with a `data` key containing only resource fields, matching the `NodePage` schema. The breadcrumb field is a PHP array of arrays, which correctly maps to the JSON array of objects expected by the schema.

The review is now checking the revision store operations. For files, the controller may return a FileRevision instead of a Node, so the spec should use FileRevisionEnvelope rather than WithContent. For documents, the operation returns a DocumentRevision without content, which means the spec likely needs DocumentRevisionEnvelope instead of WithContent.

content.thinking:
The hub URL may be null when the hub is not configured.

The schema requires `url` as a string, but the driver always emits it as `"url": null` when the hub URL is absent. This causes JSON validation to fail.

The PHPDoc explicitly permits `url` as `string|null`, but the OpenAPI spec requires a string. This creates a contract mismatch. Severity is major because the validator rejects responses containing a null URL.

The default hub URL is `ws://localhost:1234` from the environment default.

The nullable `hubUrl()` type is only for empty config. The default is a string, so the contract requiring `string` is correct. This is not a strong finding.

HubLoaded content type objects reject arrays, unlike DocumentBody. TipTap lists are unlikely. The probe prefix `vaulter.v1.__probeX` is too wide. HTTP status and body status may not be cross-checked. Next I will run tests to verify skipped streamed JSON bodies and HEAD requests.

I am now probing specific validation behaviors: unknown problem codes, date-time and allOf enforcement, oneOf null handling, additionalProperties, format date-time without timezone, empty object versus array, integer header coercion failures, media type charset, 304 responses, Cache-Control wire values, Vary documentation, Content-Language validation, golden write test logic, and shapeOf differences.

Top-level error arrays are correctly rejected by the schema. Webhook delivery status strings are acceptable without an enum. CommentSnapshot anchors may be arrays in tests, but the schema only accepts objects or null. Carbon timestamps must serialize as strings.

Content-Length string coercion to integer works correctly even when the schema is behind a `$ref`. The validator lowercases header names before lookup, so documented names like `X-Request-Id` match middleware values. Multiple Cache-Control values may be a bug.

A critical bug candidate has been identified: ETag double quoting.

The ETag string from `RepresentationTag::node()` already includes quotes. The HTTP header is set via Symfony's `setEtag`, which adds its own quotes. This confirms the double quoting bug.

Symfony's `setEtag` trims existing quotes before re-adding them, so the HTTP header is correctly single-quoted. The body etag field retains its quotes, which is acceptable since the spec does not require the same pattern there.

The design document confirms the ETag format includes quotes as part of the value, so the body field is consistent with the spec. The 304 response also sets the ETag correctly.

A potential issue with `json_encode` on header values and the Content-Disposition pattern was noted, but it is outside the current review scope.

Checking what `toJSON()` returns.

Confirmed `toJSON()` returns a string, so the schema passes. Now writing probes and starting tests. Also checking `Problem.errors` types and a spec bug in `changes.index` for 400 and 410 responses.

`nodes.purge` correctly documents 409. Many operations omit 500, but the code can emit it for any Throwable via the problem renderer.

Omitting 500 is a known gap. The spec does not use `default` responses. Contract tests would fail if production returns 500.

Production timestamps include timezone offsets, so the blind spot is not a live bug. Severity is minor because the format check is weaker than the spec claims. The negative fixture only checks "yesterday", which fails for unrelated reasons.

The `file_id` field is accepted by the contract because `additionalProperties` is open. This is a minor residual: D33/Resources forbids publishing internal fields, and the contract test should enforce that.

The unknown code finding is dropped. The schema uses examples rather than an enum, so the validator correctly treats them as annotations.

The status mismatch remains minor. A 412 response with `"status": 500` passes validation because the schema only describes status as repeating the HTTP status in prose, not as a schema constraint.

HEAD and STREAM skip body validation. This is minor for HEAD. It is more serious for STREAM: if `application/json` is on the inline allow list, a JSON file download returns a StreamedResponse with JSON content, but the contract accepts a JSON object without inspecting the body.

The streamed JSON body validation concern is hypothetical. The nodes.show endpoint is not streamed, so the schema's string type for file downloads would not be reached there.

Skipping body inspection for StreamedResponse is correct for file downloads. The body is raw bytes, not a JSON document to validate against the Node schema. No current JSON API operation uses a streamed response.

A public node with an invalid `created_at` date and a missing `Referrer-Policy` header was accepted.

Shell injection was proven in the workflow script. A malicious `base_ref` value containing `"; echo INJECTED; echo "` executed arbitrary commands and corrupted the source variable assignment.

The workflow script contains two shell interpolation sites for `base_ref` inside double quotes. This confirms the quoting defect. Severity is minor because the base branch is typically a safe value like `main`.

The injected value comes from `github.base_ref`, which is not attacker-controlled for external contributors because pull requests use the target repository's base branch. Only `github.head_ref` would be directly controllable by an attacker.

The invalid timestamp is a clearer product defect. The schema lacks a `format: date-time` constraint, so garbage values like `"not-a-date"` pass contract tests while live responses remain valid ISO strings.

The missing `Referrer-Policy` header is a minor defect because the design mandates it on every public share response. The public node timestamp issue is worse than the date-time offset hole: it has no format constraint at all, so garbage values pass contract tests. These are two distinct findings.

A quick scan is underway for other timestamp fields that lack a `format: date-time` constraint. PublicNode `created_at` and `updated_at` are the first candidates.

content.thinking: The documents test suite ran with zero assertions. This points to a bootstrap error rather than contract failures.

Drive and documents tests failed with sandbox permission denied errors. The sandbox blocks writes to Orchestra Testbench storage logs and disks.

Core OpenAPI and core HTTP suites passed. The drive and documents failures are sandbox environment limitations, not product defects.

I considered rerunning the drive and documents suites with a writable log path outside the repository, but Testbench hardcodes its storage directory inside the vendor folder. The sandbox blocks writes to that location, so the failures remain sandbox limitations.

I am checking whether the drive and documents test cases read environment variables before configuring Laravel logging. If they do, setting `LOG_CHANNEL=stderr` and a custom disk path in `/tmp` might bypass the sandbox's blocked storage directory.

The Flysystem local disk path is hardcoded to the vendor directory. No environment variable can redirect it without code changes. Core tests likely passed because they do not write files. Drive and documents tests upload files and write logs, which triggered the sandbox failures. This confirms the issue is an environment limitation, not a product defect.

No failed suites indicate a broken OpenAPI contract.

Core HTTP tests passed 150 with validation enabled, confirming core routes match the spec. The OpenAPI suite passed 38 and skipped one write-examples test. Now checking whether 500 responses are missing from the spec.

Three minor findings are now confirmed.

- The opis date-time regex accepts values without a UTC offset, violating the RFC 3339 requirement.
- PublicNode timestamps lack a format constraint, so invalid strings like "not-a-date" pass validation.
- HEAD and StreamedResponse endpoints skip body validation because no current controller returns StreamedResponse.

Two more minor findings are confirmed.

- The probe prefix is too wide: `vaulter.v1.__probeNOT` is not skipped.
- `additionalProperties` is open, so `file_id` is accepted even though the design forbids publishing it.

Three more minor findings are confirmed.

- The validator does not check that a problem body's status code matches the HTTP status.
- The contract omits Vary, so a node example without it passes.
- Public share responses may omit Referrer-Policy.

Three more minor findings are confirmed.

- The OpenAPI contract never references the 500 response, even though every route can emit it.
- CI shell quoting is broken and was injected into the repository.
- The CollaborationSession URL field is nullable in code but required in the spec; an empty URL violates the contract.

The Drive archived_at and Change shape are a minor design contradiction, but it is unclear whether this is a P6.3 defect or stale design.

The reviewer is grouping the confirmed findings to avoid inflating the minor severity count, since several are similar validator gaps.

The Drive archived_at and Change sequence fields are minor design drifts without recorded deviations. The reviewer is now weighing whether to issue a FINDINGS verdict.

The reviewer decided to issue a FINDINGS verdict. None of the confirmed issues are blockers. The PublicNode timestamp gap is minor because live responses are valid ISO strings and the core HTTP suite passed.

The probe exemption is justified because P6.2 requires those route names, so omitting it would break probe tests. The actual issue is the unseparated prefix being too wide, not the existence of any exemption.

CI base selection is correct because fetch-depth 0 includes tags. The oasdiff --fail-on ERR flag and Docker mounts are properly configured. GET and HEAD route coverage is verified. The examples write test is skipped unless the environment variable is set, so it does not produce a silent green.

ShowNodeController's properties [] deviation is correct and not a finding. allOf, oneOf, null handling, 304 bodies, charset, required headers, and content-length coercion all behave as expected. composer.lock gitignore and yaml ^8 are recorded deviations. Problem500 is defined but unused. ReferrerPolicy is required at line 3579. PublicNode created_at lacks format constraints at lines 4321-4328. ValidateOpenApiResponses is checked at lines 34 and 43-49.

The opis date-time regex is in vendor/DateTimeFormats line 24. The validator file to cite is OpenApiResponseValidator. The shell injection finding is at .github/workflows/openapi.yml lines 38-39. CollaborationSession.url is required at schema line 4931. HocuspocusCollaborationDriver hubUrl is at line 206.

The Node schema at line 4139 lacks `additionalProperties: false`, so leaked internal pointers like `file_id` pass validation. The `Vary` header is set in `ApplyResponseCachePolicy` at line 55, but the spec omits it from the `nodes.show` response headers at lines 1459-1467. The unused `Problem500` component is defined at line 3848.

The `file_id` leak is minor because OpenAPI objects are open by default, and the design never required `additionalProperties: false`. The owner may upgrade severity if they choose to harden the schema.

The problem-status mismatch is minor.

Any test failures in the documents or drive suites are sandbox issues, not product defects.

The reviewer will delete the temporary scratch files created during testing, including `/tmp/openapi-probe.php` and `/tmp/p6-*.md`, to leave no trace behind.

The problem-status mismatch is at lines 3878-3880, where the status property is typed as integer only. The Change schema at line 4662 requires node_sequence and subtree but omits seq; ChangeResource.php lines 37-44 expose this. The Drive schema at lines 4337-4347 requires a list but omits archived_at; DriveResource.php lines 34-43 expose this.

The reviewer will report the two concrete schema mismatches as a single finding to avoid noise. The Change design text may describe an older shape that was updated in code during P6.1, but the design file is the normative contract.

The design drift is minor because the spec matches the shipped resources. The reviewer will cite the OpenAPI contract as the artifact to update if the code diverges from the design.

The documents suite failed with 41 tests and zero assertions because the sandbox testbench path is not writable. A collaboration secrets warning during boot was also a sandbox logging issue, not a product defect.

The reviewer is now drafting the report. They are also removing temporary scratch files.

The probe exemption also means the catalog of problem codes is not validated against the Problem schema. A bug in a field that only some codes populate would be missed by the probe suite, though feature tests that hit those specific routes would still catch it.

The reviewer decided to split the PublicNode timestamp finding into two distinct issues: the missing date-time format constraint and the opis date-time offset hole. The probe exemption gap will be noted as a practical impact within the probe finding, but severity remains minor because real v1 routes are still validated and the core HTTP suite passed.

content.text:
VERDICT: FINDINGS

No blocker. The OpenAPI suite and the core HTTP suite pass with validation on. The gaps below are places where a response can break a P6-design promise and the adapter still accepts it, plus one workflow quoting bug.

`packages/core/tests/OpenApi`: 38 passed, 1 skipped (the examples rewrite, which stays skipped unless `VAULTER_OPENAPI_EXAMPLES_WRITE=1`), exit 0. `packages/core/tests/Http`: 150 passed, exit 0. `packages/drive/tests/Http` (123 failed, 13 passed) and `packages/documents/tests/Http` (41 failed, 0 assertions) died in this sandbox on `Permission denied` writing Testbench’s `storage/logs` and disk directories under `vendor/orchestra`. Neither log contains `breaks the OpenAPI contract`.

## Minor

**1. Public share timestamps are unconstrained strings.** `openapi/vaulter-v1.yaml:4321` and `:4325` (`PublicNode.created_at`, `updated_at`) have `type: [string, "null"]` and no `format`. Every other `*_at` field in the document is `format: date-time`. P6-design#OpenAPI requires that for times. `SharedNodeResource` emits Carbon values, so today’s responses happen to be ISO strings, and a garbage string still validates.

Reproduction: `OpenApiResponseValidator` on `public-shares.show` / 200 with `created_at: "not-a-date"`, no `Referrer-Policy`, and the three required headers (`content-type`, `x-vaulter-api-version`, `x-request-id`, `cache-control: no-store, private`) returned no violations.

**2. `format: date-time` accepts a timestamp with no offset.** Opis’s pattern marks the offset optional (`vendor/opis/json-schema/src/Formats/DateTimeFormats.php:24`). P6-design#Validators requires RFC 3339 UTC with `Z`. `SnapshotValue::iso` emits that form, so current bodies pass, and a value that drops the zone still passes. Fixture `10-malformed-timestamp.json` only substitutes `"yesterday"`, which fails the pattern for a different reason.

Reproduction: `DateTimeFormats::dateTime("2026-10-11T04:35:03")` is true. The same call on `2026-10-11T04:35:03.000000Z` is true, on `2026-02-31T00:00:00Z` is false, and on `yesterday` is false. The node example with `data.created_at` set to `2026-10-11T04:35:03` produced no validator violations.

**3. HEAD and any streamed response skip the body.** `packages/core/tests/Support/OpenApi/ValidateOpenApiResponses.php:43-49` passes `inspectBody: false` for `HEAD` and for `StreamedResponse` / `BinaryFileResponse`. Downloads are streams, so skipping their bytes is what the octet-stream schema needs. The same switch also accepts a JSON operation whose body does not match the schema.

Reproduction: a `vaulter.v1.nodes.show` response `{"data":{"id":1}}` with valid `Content-Type`, `X-Vaulter-Api-Version`, `X-Request-Id`, and `Cache-Control` headers. `terminate()` threw `AssertionFailedError` for GET. The same call with method `HEAD`, and again with a `StreamedResponse`, returned without throwing. No current JSON controller returns `StreamedResponse` (`ContentResponder::stream` is the only production stream).

**4. The probe exemption is a raw prefix.** `ValidateOpenApiResponses.php:24` and `:34` skip every route name that begins with `vaulter.v1.__probe`. That covers the real fixtures `vaulter.v1.__probe` and `vaulter.v1.__probe.node.show`. It also covers any other name with that prefix, so those responses are never checked. `DomainExceptionStatusTest` walks the catalog through `vaulter.v1.__probe`, so those problem bodies are outside the contract run.

Reproduction: the same invalid `nodes.show` body as above. `terminate()` did not throw for `vaulter.v1.__probe`, `vaulter.v1.__probe.node.show`, or `vaulter.v1.__probeNOT`. It threw for `vaulter.v1.nodes.__probe`.

**5. A leaked internal id passes, and a problem’s `status` is not tied to the HTTP status.** `Node` (`openapi/vaulter-v1.yaml:4139`) does not set `additionalProperties: false`. P6-design#Resources says `file_id` is not part of the representation. `Problem.status` (`:3878`) is only `type: integer`.

Reproduction: the committed `node` example plus `data.file_id = "internal-pointer"` produced no violations. `problem-412` with HTTP status 412 and body `status: 500`, `code: "not_a_catalog_code"` produced no violations. (`code` is `examples`, which JSON Schema does not enforce. The document test does check that the example list equals `ProblemCatalog`.)

**6. Two headers the design requires are not enforced, and `500` is never an operation response.** `ApplyResponseCachePolicy.php:55` sets `Vary: Authorization, Cookie` on an ETag response.
